Hatshepsut.myth: Khnum models Hatshepsut and her ka
Hatshepsut.note: Khnum fashions the divine royal child and her ka on his wheel.

Hededet.note: Mafdet and Hededet receive overlapping anti-venom and serpent-binding roles.
Temple theology associates or fuses Serket with the scorpion goddess Hededet.

Hedj-Wer.note: Scholars hypothesize that ibis-Thoth absorbed Hedj-Wer’s older Hermopolitan baboon form.

Hedjet.note: Hedjet is a related protective hippopotamus goddess, though her precise identification with Taweret remains disputed.

Hedjhotep.note: Hedjhotep performs his clothing function through flax produced in Hapi's fields.

Heh.note: Heh belongs to another primordial pair within Amaunet's mature Ogdoad.
Heh and Kek are co-members embodying limitless extent and primordial darkness.
Heh and Nun are male members of the standardized Ogdoad.

Heh deities.note: Ram-headed Heh figures help Shu physically support Nut.

Heket.note: Heket and Wepwawet are listed together as beneficiaries of offerings.

Hephaistos.note: Greek interpretive texts call Imouthes-Asklepios son of Hephaistos, translating his filiation to Ptah.

Hermes Trismegistos.note: Late Egyptian greatness titles and Hermes identification generate Hermes Trismegistos.

Hermopan.note: Porphyry juxtaposes universal Hermopan with composite, half-Greek Hermanubis.

Heru-ra-ha.note: Hoor-paar-kraat forms the silent, passive aspect of the composite Heru-ra-ha.

Heryshaf.note: Heryshaf is locally equated with Osiris through ram and kingship theology.

Hesat.note: Late and scholarly systematization associates Mnevis’s sacred mother-cow with Hesat.

Hittite storm gods.note: Egyptian treaty language renders foreign storm deities as forms of Sutekh.

Hoor-paar-kraat.note: Thelema reinterprets Harpocrates as the silent inward aspect of Heru-ra-ha.

Horakhty.note: Later solar liturgies combine Atum with Horakhty in cumulative solar forms.

Horit.note: Horit bears Thoth after Seth rapes her in a local tradition.

Horus Behdety.myth: Horus Behdety battles the enemies of Re
Horus Behdety.note: Nekhbet accompanies his winged disk and assists royal-solar protection.
Protective Horus presides over parallel royal imagery involving Renenutet.

Horus of Behdet.note: Horus of Behdet pursues and destroys Set and his followers.
Set's animal forms are harpooned, trampled, burned, or dismembered.

Horus of Buhen.note: He receives wine alongside Amun and Bastet-Werethekau.

Horus of Edfu.myth: Destruction of serpentiform enemies at Edfu
Horus of Edfu.note: Horus destroys enemies whose cosmic identity is assimilated to Apep.
Horus of Edfu.source: Great Horus Myth and Edfu ritual scenes

Horus of Edfu.note: Great and Lesser Enneads accompany, acclaim, and assist Horus.
Hathor journeys from Dendera to unite with Horus as his divine spouse.
Dendera theology makes Horus of Edfu Ihy’s father.

Horus of Edfu.myth: An Ogdoad-like company enters Horus's primordial prehistory
Horus of Edfu.note: Edfu appropriates an Ogdoad-like group into its local falcon god's creation theology.

Horus of Imet.note: Wadjet is the mother or senior goddess of youthful Horus within the Imet triad.

Horus of Nekhen.note: Their neighboring cult centers jointly anchor Upper Egyptian kingship.

Horus son of Isis.note: Geb is Horus’s grandfather through Osiris.

Horus son of Isis.myth: Geb adjudicates Horus’s claim against Seth
Horus son of Isis.note: Geb recognizes Horus as Osiris’s rightful heir over Seth.

Horus son of Isis.myth: Geb grants Horus the united land
Horus son of Isis.note: Geb awards Horus the whole of Egypt and confirms his inherited throne.

Horus who is in Shedet.note: They share the Medinet Madi cult complex without a preserved independent story.

Horus's four sons.myth: Judgment and protection of the dead
Horus's four sons.note: Horus's four sons stand before Osiris and protect the deceased's organs.

Horus-Hekenu.note: Nefertum is fused with Horus-Hekenu in a composite solar form.

Horus-in-his-sun-disk.note: A late witness places the hall gods' consumption of wrongdoers in his presence.

Hu.note: Hu appears among the divine tribunal above the weighing where Ammit waits.

Hu.myth: Effective faculties accompany the solar process
Hu.note: Heka supplies efficacy while Hu supplies authoritative utterance in the creator's action.
Ihy is linked with Hu and authoritative utterance in a disputed passage.
Hu, personified authoritative utterance, serves among Ra's solar crew.
Hu sits among the tribunal above the scene attended by Shai.

Iabet.note: The eastern goddess is paired with Min in traditions reflecting his orientation.

Iah.note: Thoth merges syncretically with Iah in the lunar form Iah-Thoth.

Ihy-like child musicians.note: Child musicians with sistra help welcome and calm the returning Mut.

Imsety.note: Imsety is one of the Four Sons of Horus.
A funerary variant names Imsety among the sons of Haroeris and Isis.
Nephthys appears with Imsety in the four-son and four-goddess system.

Ini-di-f.note: Mafdet leaps upon the named serpent's neck to secure the king's survival.

Io.myth: Io received upon arriving in Egypt
Io.note: Harpocrates and Isis receive Io in Egypt alongside the Nile.
Greek mythographers make Io an earlier mortal manifestation or narrative analogue of Isis.

Ipet.note: Ipet and Taweret become effectively interchangeable in some later contexts while retaining distinct local theologies.
Ipet.source: Late Egyptian temple and funerary evidence

Irer.note: Irer is listed with Hu, Sia, Heka, and Sedjem as a creative or operative faculty.

Irta.note: Irta generates or mediates the generation of the Eight.

Irta.myth: Irta generates the Eight in Theban cosmogony
Irta.note: A later Theban creator form connects Kematef to the Eight and living Amun.

Isis of Philae.note: Local divine companies incorporating Osirian gods center upon Isis.

Isis-Thermouthis.note: Isis-Thermouthis shares Dendera's late maternal-fertility system without universally being Hathor.

Iunit.note: Iunit joins an expanded local Ennead in Theban theology.

Iunyt.note: Iunyt appears with Montu and Tjenenet in Armant theology.

Kematef.note: The pair descend directly or through Irta from Kematef.
The deceased Ogdoad rest with Kematef beneath Djeme’s sacred mound.

Kematef.myth: Kematef precedes the Eight in Theban creation
Kematef.note: Theban theology presents Kematef as a primordial ancestor or generator of the Eight.

Kematef.myth: Kematef and the Eight rest at Djeme
Kematef.note: The primeval serpent rests with the completed creator-gods at their sacred necropolis.

Khensit.note: Khensit is Sopdu’s local consort, although no developed marriage narrative survives.

Khentamentiu.note: Middle Kingdom stelae place Khentamentiu and Wepwawet within the same festival and offering environment.

Khentiamentiu.note: Anubis can bear Khentiamentiu’s name or title amid historical titular absorption.
Osiris absorbs the earlier Abydene funerary god Khentiamentiu and assumes his title.

Khenty-irty.note: Later Letopolitan theology fuses Haroeris with the sighted-and-blind falcon eye god.

Khereduankh.note: Late monuments name the human or divinized Khereduankh as Imhotep's mother.

Kherseket.note: Local Komir theology permits Anuket to be qualified as Kherseket.

Kherty.myth: Kherty ferries the king identified as Sokar
Kherty.note: Kherty supplies transport for the dead king after he assumes Sokar's identity.

Khnum-Re.note: Khnum-Re guards the cataract while Satis burns the southern enemy.
Khnum-Re.source: Book of the Victory over Seth

Khonsu-pȝ-jr-sḫr.note: Khonsu-in-Thebes Neferhotep grants protective power to this traveling manifestation.

Khonsu-the-Child.note: Temple theology juxtaposes or assimilates Harpocrates with Khonsu’s child form.

Kneph.note: Through Agathos Daimon, Shai's later complex is identified with primeval serpent Kneph.

Kolanthes.note: Kolanthes is the child of Min-Re and Repyt at Athribis.

Kronos.note: Greco-Roman interpretation equates Geb with the old divine king Kronos.
Greek documents render the composite Soknebtunis-Geb as Soknebtunis-Kronos.

Kuk.note: They are fellow Ogdoad members representing boundlessness and darkness.

Maga.note: Maga is a crocodilian son or manifestation of Set.

Mahes.note: Bubastite and Leontopolitan temple theology makes the lion god Bastet’s son.

Mandulis.note: Mandulis and Isis receive devotion within the same Nubian-Egyptian sanctuary environment.

Matet.note: Matet escorts Isis during her flight with the child Horus.

Matit.note: Mehit and Matit stand symmetrically as lioness guardians of Osiris.

Mehen.myth: Protecting Re during the nocturnal journey
Mehen.note: Heka and Mehen belong among the protective beings enabling Re's nightly passage.

Mehet-Weret.note: Some late compilations attribute Heka's motherhood to Mehet-Weret, though documentation is weak.
Neith assumes the identity of the primordial flood and celestial cow.
Both goddesses can embody the heavenly cow and solar birth.

Mehet-Weret.myth: Solar emergence from the celestial cow
Mehet-Weret.note: Ra emerges from Mehet-Weret or is carried by her as celestial cow.
Sobek emerges from her leg and tail, though the maternal interpretation is debated.

Mehetweret.note: Late temple theology occasionally assimilates Iusaaset to Mehetweret.

Mehyt.note: Mehyt is Anhur’s paired lioness goddess and later consort.
Anhur brings the distant lioness Mehyt back from the desert or Nubia.
Mehyt becomes consort of Shu through his regional fusion with Onuris.
As Onuris-Shu, Shu retrieves the distant lioness Mehyt and brings her home.
Mehyt can occupy the returning Solar Eye role pacified by Thoth.

Menhyt.note: Menhyt is Heka the Child's mother in a principal Esna genealogy.
Menhyt is Khnum’s consort or female partner within Esna’s divine family.

Merit-Re.note: Werethekau and Merit-Re are invoked together in the District of Kheput.

Meskhenet.myth: Birth of Reddjedet’s three royal sons
Meskhenet.note: Meskhenet proclaims each newborn’s destiny after Heqet hastens delivery.
Nephthys attends the births while Meskhenet declares the infants' destinies.
They appear together near the balance, linking birth allotment with final judgment.
Meskhenet stands with Shai and Renenutet beside the balance.

Meskhent.note: Meskhent-related birth powers attend the delivery and recognition scenes.

Mestet.note: Mestet escorts Isis during her flight with the child Horus.

Mestetef.note: Mestetef escorts Isis during her flight with the child Horus.

Minoan genius.myth: Taweret imagery becomes the Minoan genius
Minoan genius.note: Cretan artists adapted Taweret's visual form into a locally transformed ritual being.

Morning Star.note: A divinized morning star is born from Sopdet’s union with the king or Osiris.

Msḫtyw.myth: Celestial opposition between southern and northern constellations
Msḫtyw.note: Astronomical arrangements place Sopdet and Sah opposite or protected from the northern Foreleg constellation.

Naneferkaptah.note: Thoth complains to Re after Naneferkaptah takes his book, bringing catastrophe upon the family.

Nebethetepet.note: Nebethetepet is paired with Atum as the receptive female component of creation.
Hathor is locally identified with Atum's female generative hand, Nebethetepet.
Compound names fuse Iusaaset and Nebethetepet into a single divine form.
They appear as distinct paired goddesses protecting enthroned Re-Horakhty.
Nebethetepet is a female counterpart of Atum-Ra's generative hand.

Nebetu.note: Nebetu belongs to Khnum’s local divine circle and shares liturgical worship.

Nebtu.note: Nebtu is an alternative or coexisting mother of Heka at Esna.

Nehebkau.note: Nehebkau appears as one member of the assessor roster.
Some mortuary traditions make the serpent Nehebkau a son of Geb.
Renenutet is named as Nehebkau’s mother, with Geb as father.
Pyramid Text material gives Serket a maternal and nurturing relation to Nehebkau.
Nehebkau sees Serket within ritual statements supporting the king’s ascent.

Nehemetawy.note: Later Hermopolitan theology pairs Nehemetawy with Thoth as his consort.

Neilos.note: Greek and Roman traditions translated Hapi's sacred inundation into the classical river god Neilos or Nilus.

Nepherses.note: Isis is regionally associated or identified with Nepherses.

Nepri.note: Nepri's grain and Hapi's flood jointly express royal provisioning and agricultural abundance.
Later tradition treats the grain god as her child and celebrates his birth.

Niau.myth: Changing rosters of the primordial Eight
Niau.note: Niau belongs to a pair that can replace Amun and Amaunet.
Niau belongs to an alternative fourth pair associated with emptiness or negation.
Niau joins Kek in a regional roster representing emptiness or negation.
Niau substitutes into some Theban Ogdoad lists alongside Nun.

Niaut.myth: Changing rosters of the primordial Eight
Niaut.note: Niaut belongs to a pair that can replace Amun and Amaunet.
Niaut belongs to an alternative fourth pair associated with emptiness or negation.
Niaut joins Kek in a regional roster representing emptiness or negation.
Niaut substitutes into some Theban Ogdoad lists alongside Naunet.

Nilus.note: Serapis and the personified Nile receive joint dedications.
Serapis governs the Nile's inundation and is regarded as its author.

Osiris of Mendes.note: Osiris of Mendes shares the divine land-grant scene with Harpocrates.

Ouranos.note: Greco-Roman comparison links both as sky embodiments despite differing gender and functions.

Pachimesen.note: Spiegelberg proposed fusion with Shai, but recent excavators retain separate identities.

Pakhet.note: The local lioness goddess appears as Pakhet-Werethekau in a coronation scene.

Panebtawy.note: Panebtawy is the child of Haroeris and Tasenetnofret at Kom Ombo.

Petet.note: Petet escorts Isis during her flight with the child Horus.

Pre-Harakhty.note: Babi declares his shrine vacant, causing Pre-Harakhty to withdraw in distress.

Ptah-Tatenen.note: Ptah-Tatenen and Khepri are co-invoked in Isis's appeal.

Qebehsenuef.note: Qebehsenuef is one of the Four Sons of Horus.
A funerary variant names Qebehsenuef among the sons of Haroeris and Isis.
Nephthys appears with Qebehsenuef in the four-son and four-goddess system.
Serket protects and embraces Qebehsenuef, who guards the intestines.
Qebehsenuef accompanies Horus in the episode, without clear independent action involving Sobek.
Qebehsenuef.source: Coffin Text 158; Book of the Dead 113

Qebehut.note: Qebehut is identified as Anubis’s daughter; her mother is unspecified.

Qudshu.note: Qudshu occupies an erotic-fertility field overlapping Hathor, sometimes with Min and Reshep.
Min flanks Qudshu alongside Resheph in healing or devotional imagery.

Ra-Hoor.myth: Midnight passage in the solar bark
Ra-Hoor.note: Crowley's ritual places Ra-Hoor at the helm of Khephra's bark.

Ra-Hoor-Khuit.note: Thelemic cosmology pairs silent Hoor-paar-kraat with Ra-Hoor-Khuit.

Ra-Hoor-Khuit.myth: Thelemic union of Nuit and Hadit
Ra-Hoor-Khuit.note: The union of Nuit and Hadit generates Ra-Hoor-Khuit in Thelemic theology.

Ra-Horakhty.note: Depending on ritual grammar, Hathor can be Ra-Horakhty's daughter or Eye.
Some ritual systems make Hathor Ra-Horakhty's consort or feminine complement.
Some ritual arrangements treat Hathor as Ra-Horakhty's maternal source.

Ra-Horakhty.myth: Hathor and the laughing solar judge
Ra-Horakhty.note: Hathor exposes herself, making the angry solar judge laugh and resume judgment.
Ra-Horakhty sits among the tribunal above the scene attended by Shai.

Ra/Re.note: The sun enters Nut at evening and is born from her at dawn.

Raet-Tawy.note: Raet-Tawy is Montu-Re's consort and female solar counterpart.

Ramesses II.note: A probable Mehit presents the divine king Ramesses II with a menat.
Ramesses II.source: Ramesses II temple relief at Abydos

Ramesses II.note: The divine king is reportedly styled lord of Shai, though the primary locus is insecure.
Ramesses II.source: Royal inscription reported by Maspero and Budge

Rat-Tawy.note: Rat-Tawy personifies a female Ra within Theban-region solar theology.

Rat-tawy.note: Local temple theology names Rat-tawy as Thoth’s mother.

Re.note: Through identification with Shu, Anhur is systematized as Re’s son.
Anhur defends Re against enemies threatening divine and cosmic order.
Anhur restores Re’s distant solar Eye by escorting the goddess home.
Solar Eye theology classifies Anuket as a protective daughter of Re.
Atum fuses with Re as a combined solar creator and sovereign.
Atum confronts and disables Re's bound serpent enemy during the nocturnal passage.
Atum is enumerated as a form or nocturnal phase of Re.

Re.myth: Power over water in the realm of the dead
Re.note: The deceased as Babi is the oar with which Re rows.
Re rejects Baba’s accusation and hands him to Thoth for punishment.
Polymorphic Bes-images incorporate solar insignia and present him as a cosmic protector.
Re presides over, debates with, and becomes angered at the tribunal.
Spell 125C associates the judgment ordeal's purification with Re's crew.
Solar theology presents Hapi's inundation and greening as operating under Re's cosmic authority.
Re.source: Hymn to Hapi and solar hymns

Re.note: Solar theology can present Re as the divine child’s solar father.

Re.myth: Newborn sun rises from the lotus
Re.note: Harpocrates embodies the newborn or daily reborn sun.

Re.myth: Poisoning and healing in the marshes
Re.note: Some healing variants make Re or his solar authority instrumental in the cure.
Solar-Eye theology calls Hathor the daughter and emitted power of Re.
Re.source: Middle Kingdom and later temple texts

Re.note: Hathor can function as Re's consort-like feminine complement.
As Re's Eye, Hathor attacks rebellious humanity and defends his rule.
Re ends Hathor's slaughter by flooding fields with blood-colored beer.
Heka is identified as Re's ba, his manifested magical potency.
Later theology identifies Heka as Re's ka or vital essence.
Heka accompanies and protects Re during his nocturnal solar progress.

Re.myth: Birth of Reddjedet’s three royal sons
Re.note: Re commissions Heqet and four other deities to deliver the triplets.
Kom Ombo theology calls Haroeris the son of Re.
Kom Ombo theology solarizes Haroeris and treats Re as an identity or source.
The Eight collectively bring forth, parent, elevate, or greet Re.
Re is the likely solar father whose height the newborn Ihy reaches.
Ihy accompanies Re in heaven and on earth without perishing.
The deceased bears both Re’s name and Ihy’s name.
Kek and the Eight collectively generate, protect, or renew the sun god.
In solarized theology, Re can function as Khonsu's father.
Khonsu is solarized as Khonsu-Re and assumes Re-Horakhty's form and insignia.
Late Eye-goddess theology calls Mehit the leonine daughter of Re.
Mehit functions as Re's protective Eye and uraeus after her return.
Meretseger is titled Daughter of Re through Eye-of-Re and uraeus theology.
Re.source: TT 106, tomb of Paser, Pillar H

Re.note: Mnevis serves as Re’s terrestrial herald and representative.
Later theology describes Mnevis as Re’s ba or living manifestation.
Montu fused with Re as a solar deity.
Mut bears the functional solar-genealogy title Daughter of Re.
As Re’s Eye, Mut attacks enemies, withdraws, returns, and is pacified.
Re.source: Temple texts and Hymn to Mut

Re.note: Nefertum is Re's fragrant flower and appears with his daily emergence.
The deceased as Nefertum supplies Re with fragrant renewal and purification.
As Re's Eye and protective uraeus, she stands against rebels.
Re commands Nephthys and four other deities to assist Ruddjedet.

Re.myth: The Eight bring forth the first sun
Re.note: The Eight generate or reveal Re as the newborn solar creator.

Re.myth: The Eight acclaim the first sunrise
Re.note: The Eight protect, worship, and greet the newborn sun, sometimes as baboons.
Later solar theology calls Satis a daughter and aggressive Eye of Re.
Seshat records the royal eternity authorized or supplied by the solar deity.
Re.source: New Kingdom and later temple inscriptions

Re.note: Shai becomes a name or manifestation of the solar creator Re.
Shu is called Re's son where Atum is solarized or replaced by Re.
Shu supports Re's solar journey, appears in his bark, and raises the sun.
Learned chronologies make Shu the earthly ruler succeeding Re.
Re questions and instructs Sobek about the hands, fish-trap, and ritual consequences.
Re.source: Coffin Text 158; Book of the Dead 113

Re.note: Sobek is fused with Re as Sobek-Re, acquiring solar and creator attributes.
Re.source: Middle and New Kingdom religious sources

Re.myth: Re traverses Sokar's sandy underworld realm
Re.note: Re's nocturnal passage animates Sokar's hidden corpse-region and enables renewal.
At the horizon Sopdet can be described as Re’s mother.
Sopdet rises before Re and nurses the sun at the horizon.
A Hibis inscription calls Sopdet the Eye of Re.
Re addresses or recognizes the transformed king as Sopdu within eastern celestial theology.
Ptah-Tatenen produces the sun, whose eyes dispel primordial darkness.
Solar-Eye theology makes Tefnut the daughter and active Eye of Re.
Tefnut leaves Re or Egypt, and Re summons his estranged Eye home.

Re-Atum.note: Re-Atum requests Neith's ruling when the divine tribunal remains deadlocked.

Re-Harakhty.note: Re-Harakhty appears on the funerary stela of a priest of Montu.

Re-Horakhty.myth: Harpist worship in Ramesses III’s tomb
Re-Horakhty.note: Anhur-Shu and Re-Horakhty jointly receive a harpist’s cultic performance.
The early didactic name explicitly incorporated Re-Horakhty into Aten's identity.
Re-Horakhty's name was removed when Aten's titulary became more exclusive.
Iusaaset and Nebethetepet stand beside the enthroned solar god protectively.
Re-Horakhty emerges as the child sun from the Ogdoad’s lotus.

Re-Horakhty.myth: Re-Horakhty emerges from the egg or lotus
Re-Horakhty.note: A regional version makes Re-Horakhty the solar child produced by the Eight.

Re/Ra.note: Apis’s solar disk and uraeus assimilate him to royal-solar potency.

Renpetneferet.note: One unstable late tradition presents Renpetneferet as Imhotep's sister.
An alternative unstable tradition presents Renpetneferet as Imhotep's wife.

Repyt.note: Repyt is the wife of Min-Re in the Athribis triad.

Rerek.note: Mafdet severs the head of the seven-cubit serpent that consumes spirits.

Reret.note: Reret shares Taweret's hippopotamus form and protective functions, especially in astronomical and funerary systems.

Rhamnusia.note: Rhamnusia is named among the foreign manifestations of universal Isis.

Ruty.myth: Aker’s opposed form overlaps with Ruty
Ruty.note: Aker’s double earth form is iconographically and conceptually assimilated to Ruty.
Ruty.source: Middle and New Kingdom funerary tradition

Ruty.note: Ruty appears as the Double Lion, one member of the roster.

Sah.myth: Sopdet guides Sah and the deceased along celestial paths
Sah.note: Sopdet accompanies Sah and leads him and the deceased onto the sky’s perfect paths.
Sah.source: Pyramid Texts, PT 442 and related recensions

Sah.myth: Sah and Sopdet encircle the deceased
Sah.note: Sopdet and Sah jointly encircle or escort the deceased.
Later astral theology presents Sah as Sopdet’s husband or consort.
Sah functions as Sopdu’s father within the astral family of Sah, Sopdet, and Sopdu.
Sah.source: Pyramid Text and later astral theology

Sarapis.note: Alexandrian coins show Hermanubis beside or facing enthroned Sarapis.

Satet.note: Some monuments fuse Sopdet with Satet through shared celestial, inundation, and iconographic functions.

Satet.myth: Satet follows Sopdet’s cow in inundation procession
Satet.note: Satet follows the Dendera Sopdet cow in an astronomical procession signifying inundation.

Sedjem.note: Sedjem is listed with Hu, Sia, Heka, and Irer as a personified sensory and creative faculty.

Sefkhet-Abwy.note: Their names and images alternate, pair, or combine as closely related manifestations.
Sefkhet-Abwy.source: Middle Kingdom through Ptolemaic temple texts

Serqet.note: Serqet joins the divine forces protecting and healing the child from venom.

Setna.note: Setna suffers supernatural deception after taking Thoth’s book and eventually returns it.

Shed.note: Harpocrates absorbs or overlaps Shed’s earlier protective child and dangerous-animal iconography.
Child Horus absorbs Shed's mastery over dangerous animals.

Shepsi.note: Shepsi appears as the local solar child produced by the Eight.

Shepsi.myth: Shepsi appears as the child of the Eight
Shepsi.note: The local Hermopolitan solar god replaces Re as child of the Eight.

Shesemu.note: Shesemu produces oils from the agricultural abundance supplied by Hapi.

Shesmetet.myth: Conception and birth of the deceased king
Shesmetet.note: Sekhmet conceives the king while Shesmetet gives birth to him.
Some disputed local traditions call Shesmetet Sopdu’s mother, separately from the astral genealogy involving Sopdet.

Sobek-Re.note: Khonsu is the child of Sobek-Re in the local Kom Ombo family.

Sokar-Osiris.note: The deceased sage is invoked in a transfigured Osirian form as Sokar-Osiris Imhotep.

Sol.myth: Roman interpretation of Egyptian solar gods
Sol.note: Roman observers interpreted Ra and related Egyptian solar beings through Sol.

Sole Lord.note: The solitary creator makes Heka before differentiated existence.
Heka guards and effectuates the command ordained by the creator.

Taboubu.note: Modern scholars suggest Taboubu may manifest Bastet, but the tale never explicitly identifies them.

Tasenetnofret.note: She is Haroeris’s principal local consort in the Kom Ombo triad.

Teal'c.note: Teal'c kills the fictional Goa'uld Amaunet.

Tefen.note: Tefen escorts Isis during her flight with the child Horus.

Tenem.myth: Changing rosters of the primordial Eight
Tenem.note: Tenem belongs to an earlier alternative pair in changing Eight traditions.
Tenem belongs to an alternative fourth pair replacing Amun and Amaunet.
Tenem joins Kek in a regional roster representing wandering or disappearance.
Tenem replaces Amun in an eightfold primordial enumeration containing Nun.

Tenemet.myth: Changing rosters of the primordial Eight
Tenemet.note: Tenemet belongs to an earlier alternative pair in changing Eight traditions.
Tenemet belongs to an alternative fourth pair replacing Amun and Amaunet.
Tenemet replaces Amunet in an eightfold primordial enumeration containing Naunet.

Tenemut.note: Tenemut joins Kek in a regional roster representing wandering or disappearance.

The Eldest Magician.myth: Binding Apep in the seventh hour
The Eldest Magician.note: The Eldest Magician joins Isis in neutralizing Apep’s strength.

The Seven Arrows.note: Sekhmet commands or manifests plague-bearing arrows and messengers.

The two Maat-goddesses.myth: Personification of the Hall of the Two Maat
The two Maat-goddesses.note: Paired Maat figures sometimes personify the hall occupied by the assessors.

Thermouthis.note: Isis is fused with the serpent-form harvest goddess Thermouthis.

Thetet.note: Thetet escorts Isis during her flight with the child Horus.

Tjenenet.note: Tjenenet joins an expanded local Ennead in Theban theology.
Tjenenet is Montu's consort or companion at Tod and Armant.

Triphis.note: An archaic carrying-chair image of Repyt includes a Bat emblem, but the connection is indirect.

Tutu.note: Bes and Tutu jointly appear as protectors who subdue hostile powers.

Unas.note: Khonsu slaughters and disembowels divine victims for the deified king Unas.
Mafdet acts through and for the divine king, securing his survival.

Wadjet/Eye of Horus.note: Set tears out or damages Horus's divine eye.

phoenix.note: Greek reception interprets Bennu through a distinct Heliopolitan sacred phoenix tradition.

the Eye of Atum/Re.note: Atum sends his personified Eye to find his children in Nun.
Atum pacifies the returning Eye and exalts it upon his forehead as the uraeus.

the Harsesis child.note: The fictional Amaunet bears the Harsesis child.

the Nile.myth: Io received upon arriving in Egypt
the Nile.note: The personified Nile joins Harpocrates and Isis in receiving Io.

the Seven Hathors.note: The Seven Hathors are a collective plurality or sevenfold manifestation of Hathor.

the Sons of Horus.note: The Sons of Horus occur in Apis burial decoration and embalming theology.
They jointly appear with Nekhbet in coffin programs guarding the deceased.

the Two Lions.myth: Primordial paired powers invoked for Unas
the Two Lions.note: The Two Lions appear with Atum after Amun and Amaunet.

the gods.note: Khonsu slaughters the unnamed gods whom Unas subsequently consumes.
Late theology makes Khonsu participate in the primordial production of the gods.
Late creator theology praises Mut as the mother who birthed the gods.

the great ones of the northern sky.note: They cook divine victims after Khonsu performs the slaughter and evisceration.

the hostile spirit of Bentresh.note: Khonsu confronts the spirit, which recognizes him, bargains for a feast, and departs.

the pursuing serpent.myth: Serpent pursues Thueris after her defection
the pursuing serpent.note: An unnamed serpent pursues Thueris until Horus's followers cut it apart.
